Muslims, Jews and Christians are like labourers hired for parts of a day; the Muslims, working from Asr to sunset, get double pay, which Allah calls His blessing.
Allah will oppose three on Resurrection Day: one who betrays a covenant made in His name, one who sells a free person, and one who withholds a labourer's wages.
Labourers who quit at midday and at Asr forfeit their wages, while a last batch working till sunset receives both batches' wages; such are the Muslims, who accepted the guidance.
Three men trapped in a cave by a rock invoke Allah by deeds done for His sake: serving parents, leaving a cousin untouched and paying a labourer's grown wages.
When told to give in charity, the companions worked as porters in the market to earn a Mudd, though some later owned a hundred thousand.
The Prophet forbade meeting caravans on the way and a townsman selling for a bedouin, which Ibn Abbas explains as acting as his broker.
Al-As bin Wail will not pay Khabbab unless he disbelieves in Muhammad, promising to pay after resurrection with property and offspring, and a verse is revealed about such a man.
Companions refused hospitality recite Al-Fatiha as Ruqya over a stung chief for a flock of sheep, and the Prophet approves and asks for a share.
The Prophet was cupped and paid the cupper his wages in foodstuff, asking his masters to reduce his tax, and he never withheld anyone's wages.
The Prophet forbade the price of a dog, the earnings of prostitutes and slave-girls by prostitution, a soothsayer's charges, and payment for an animal's copulation.
The Prophet gave Khaibar's land to the Jews to farm for half its yield until Umar evacuated them, while Rafi says the Prophet forbade renting farms.
A rich man delaying repayment is unjust, and a debt transferred to a rich debtor should be accepted; the Prophet prays over a debtor once Abu Qatada takes it on.
Sureties are taken for an adulterer already lashed and for repentant renegades; an Israelite borrower names Allah as witness and surety, and his repayment reaches the lender by sea.
The Prophet's bond of brotherhood let emigrants inherit from Ansar until verse 4.33 ended that; he joined Abdur-Rahman bin Auf with Sa'd and allied Quraish with the Ansar.
The Prophet will not lead a debtor's funeral prayer until Abu Qatada undertakes to pay the debt.
Abu Bakr pays Jabir the Bahrain money the Prophet had promised; in Mecca he returns Ibn Ad-Daghna's protection, content with Allah's, and waits to emigrate with the Prophet.
The Prophet prayed over dead debtors only if they left enough to repay; once wealthy through conquests, he took on believers' debts, their wealth going to their heirs.
Ali distributes the saddles and skins of the slaughtered Budn, and Uqba, left with a kid after sharing out sheep, is told to sacrifice it himself.
Abdur-Rahman bin Auf, under a written pact with Umaiya bin Khalaf, tries to shield him at Badr, but Bilal calls the Ansar, who kill Umaiya and his son.
The Prophet forbids exchanging two Sa of poor dates for one of good Janib dates as Riba: sell the poor dates for money and buy with it.
A slave-girl slaughters a dying sheep with a broken stone, and the Prophet permits eating it.
A creditor, rude in one report, is given an older camel than he was owed, and the Prophet says the best people repay others' rights generously.
The Hawazin delegation, now Muslim, choose their captives over their property, and the Prophet asks the Muslims to return them; their chiefs confirm all gave up their shares willingly.
The Prophet buys Jabir's slow camel, letting him ride it to Medina, approves his marrying a widow to care for his father's daughters, and has Bilal pay extra.
A woman offers herself to the Prophet, and he marries her to a man who asks, for what he knows of the Quran by heart.
Caught thrice stealing the Ramadan Sadaqa, a thief teaches Abu Huraira to recite Ayat al-Kursi at bedtime for protection; the Prophet says he told the truth but was Satan.
Bilal exchanges two Sa of poor dates for one of Barni dates, and the Prophet says it is Riba: sell the poor dates for money, then buy.
The trustee of Umar's Waqf may eat from it and feed friends without amassing wealth; Ibn Umar managed it and gave presents from it.
The Prophet sends Unais to stone a man's wife if she confesses illegal sexual intercourse, and has those present beat a drunk man with shoes and palm-leaf stalks.
Aisha twisted garlands for the Prophet's sacrificial animals, which he sent with her father, and nothing lawful became unlawful for him until they were slaughtered.
Hearing verse 3.92, Abu Talha gives his beloved garden Beeruha in charity and the Prophet suggests he divide it among relatives; an honest treasurer is one of two charitable persons.
Whatever a bird, person or animal eats of what a Muslim plants counts as charity, yet Abu Umama heard the Prophet say humiliation enters any house farming equipment enters.
Keeping a dog not guarding farms or cattle, or hunting, costs a Qirat of reward daily; a cow says it was made for ploughing, and a wolf speaks.
The Prophet declines to divide the Ansar's palms with the emigrants, who instead tend the trees and share the fruit.
The Prophet had the palms of Bani An-Nadir burnt and cut down at Al-Buwaira, as a poem of Hassan bin Thabit recalls.
Renting land for one portion's yield is forbidden; the Prophet let Khaibar's people farm for half its produce, and Ibn Abbas says lending land free is better than renting it.
Three men shut in a cave by a rock invoke Allah by deeds done for His sake, and Allah removes the rock.
Umar would have divided conquered land among the soldiers, as the Prophet did Khaibar, but for later generations; whoever cultivates land belonging to nobody has most right to it.
At Dhul-Hulaifa in the valley of Al-Aqiq the Prophet is told in a dream it is a blessed valley, where he should pray and intend Umrah with Hajj.
Khaibar's Jews farmed for half its fruit until Umar expelled them; Rafi says the Prophet forbade renting farms for produce, Ibn Abbas that lending free is better.
